findings.heading: `na.omit()`
findings.proposition: Applied to a data frame, na.omit() removes rows that have ANY missing value; the French states it removes rows whose values are ALL missing ("les lignes dont *toutes* les valeurs sont manquantes").
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader believes na.omit(linelist) keeps every partially incomplete row and only drops fully empty rows. They will run it expecting almost no rows to be lost, and silently lose the large majority of the linelist, or wrongly conclude the function is broken.

findings.heading: `drop_na()`
findings.proposition: drop_na() with no arguments removes rows with ANY missing value; the French states it removes rows whose values are ALL missing ("elle supprime également les lignes dont *toutes* les valeurs sont manquantes").
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader mis-predicts the size of the filtered data set and cannot reconcile the row count printed by the very next chunk in the chapter (linelist %>% drop_na() %>% nrow()), which drops rows on ANY missingness.

findings.heading: Types de donnees manquantes / Types of missing data
findings.proposition: The English says imputing MCAR data is often fairly simple; the French says imputing MA (its abbreviation for MAR) data is relatively simple, and contrasts it only with MOP (MNAR).
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader takes MAR data to be the easy case and loses the chapter's actual ranking of difficulty (MCAR easy, MAR intermediate and the assumption of most methods, MNAR hard). The same segment then says most common methods assume MA, which now reads as a tautology instead of the intended contrast.

findings.heading: Imputation par la moyenne / Mean Imputation
findings.proposition: The English justifies mean imputation by an assumption of MCAR (twice: for the general case and for the missing temperature measurements); the French substitutes MA, its abbreviation for MAR, in both places.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader applies mean imputation to data they believe are MAR, which the chapter elsewhere describes as systematically and predictably missing. Mean imputation under MAR is biased, and the reader has been told the opposite by the text that introduces it.

findings.heading: `NA`
findings.proposition: The French adds a gloss that NA stands for "Non available"; the English never expands the abbreviation.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader learns an expansion the English does not give, and the form given is not the R documentation's wording ("Not Available"), so a reader who repeats it is quoting something no R source says.

findings.heading: Types de donnees manquantes / Types of missing data
findings.proposition: The French MCAR definition adds that missingness is also unrelated to unmeasured variables ("ou avec des variables non mesurees"); the English restricts the statement to the other variables in your data.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader is given a stronger definition of MCAR than the English chapter states, so the two language versions disagree on what a reader must be able to assume before analysing non-missing data without imputation.

findings.heading: Types de donnees manquantes / Types of missing data
findings.proposition: The French calls the MNAR mechanism "non-ignorable" ("Ce mecanisme de non-reponse est _non-ignorable_"); the English introduces no such term.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader meets a technical term with no definition and no counterpart in the English chapter, and cannot look it up anywhere else in the handbook.

findings.heading: Imputation par regression / Regression imputation
findings.proposition: The English states that predictions are produced only for observations where temperature is missing but age and fever are NOT missing; the French drops the condition on the predictors.
findings.reader_consequence: A French reader expects predictions_for_missing_temps to cover every row with a missing temperature, and is not warned that rows also missing age or fever get no imputed value.
